claim: mTOR is a key protein kinase controlling cellular metabolism and growth
source: The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a key protein kinase controlling cellular metabolism and growth.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about mTOR function

claim: mTOR is part of two structurally and functionally distinct multiprotein complexes mTORC1 and mTORC2
source: It is part of the two structurally and functionally distinct multiprotein complexes mTORC1 and mTORC2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Dysregulation of mTOR occurs in diabetes, cancer and neurological disease
source: Dysregulation of mTOR occurs in diabetes, cancer and neurological disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: The architecture of human mTORC2 was determined at intermediate resolution
source: We report the architecture of human mTORC2 at intermediate resolution, revealing a conserved binding site for accessory proteins on mTOR and explaining the structural basis for the rapamycin insensitivity of the complex.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript

claim: Human mTORC2 structure reveals a conserved binding site for accessory proteins on mTOR
source: We report the architecture of human mTORC2 at intermediate resolution, revealing a conserved binding site for accessory proteins on mTOR and explaining the structural basis for the rapamycin insensitivity of the complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The structure explains the structural basis for the rapamycin insensitivity of mTORC2
source: We report the architecture of human mTORC2 at intermediate resolution, revealing a conserved binding site for accessory proteins on mTOR and explaining the structural basis for the rapamycin insensitivity of the complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: mTOR is the master regulator of cellular growth
source: The serine/threonine kinase mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) is the master regulator of cellular growth (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support

claim: TOR was originally identified in yeast
source: Originally identified in yeast as TOR (Heitman et al., 1991; Kunz et al., 1993), the mammalian orthologue mTOR senses a range of cellular cues, including nutrient and energy availability, and growth factor signals, to control metabolism and autophagy (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012; Loewith and Hall, 2011; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support from the original discovery papers

claim: mTOR senses nutrient and energy availability and growth factor signals to control metabolism and autophagy
source: Originally identified in yeast as TOR (Heitman et al., 1991; Kunz et al., 1993), the mammalian orthologue mTOR senses a range of cellular cues, including nutrient and energy availability, and growth factor signals, to control metabolism and autophagy (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012; Loewith and Hall, 2011; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support

claim: Aberrant mTOR signaling is observed in major diseases
source: Due to its role as a central controller of cell growth, aberrant mTOR signaling is observed in major diseases (Dazert and Hall, 2011; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support

claim: mTOR is a member of the phosphatidylinositol-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) family
source: mTOR is a member of the phosphatidylinositol-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) family (Keith and Schreiber, 1995) and exerts its function as the enzymatic component of two distinct protein complexes, mTOR complex (mTORC) one and mTORC2.
evidence: This is stated with citation support

claim: mTOR exerts its function as the enzymatic component of two distinct protein complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2
source: mTOR is a member of the phosphatidylinositol-kinase-related kinase (PIKK) family (Keith and Schreiber, 1995) and exerts its function as the enzymatic component of two distinct protein complexes, mTOR complex (mTORC) one and mTORC2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: mTOR forms the core of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 together with the small protein mLST8
source: Together with the small protein mLST8, mTOR forms the core of both complexes (Kim et al., 2003; Loewith et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation support

claim: Raptor is unique to mTORC1
source: The protein Raptor is unique to mTORC1 (Hara et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2002), whereas the proteins Rictor and SIN1 are defining subunits of mTORC2 (Frias et al., 2006; Jacinto et al., 2006; Jacinto et al., 2004; Sarbassov et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support

claim: Rictor and SIN1 are defining subunits of mTORC2
source: The protein Raptor is unique to mTORC1 (Hara et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2002), whereas the proteins Rictor and SIN1 are defining subunits of mTORC2 (Frias et al., 2006; Jacinto et al., 2006; Jacinto et al., 2004; Sarbassov et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support

claim: Protor-1/2 and Deptor can bind to mTORC2
source: Additionally, Protor-1/2 and Deptor can bind to mTORC2 (Pearce et al., 2007; Peterson et al., 2009).

claim: Rapamycin in complex with FKBP12 inhibits mTORC1 activity by binding the FRB domain of mTOR
source: The polyketide rapamycin, in complex with the endogenous protein FKBP12, inhibits mTORC1 activity by binding the FKBP-rapamycin (FRB) domain of mTOR (Aylett et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2013).

claim: The FKBP-rapamycin complex is unable to bind mTORC2
source: In contrast, the FKBP-rapamycin complex is unable to bind mTORC2 (Jacinto et al., 2004), although prolonged rapamycin treatment disrupts mTORC2 signaling by preventing mTOR incorporation into mTORC2 (Lamming et al., 2012; Sarbassov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support

claim: Prolonged rapamycin treatment disrupts mTORC2 signaling by preventing mTOR incorporation into mTORC2
source: In contrast, the FKBP-rapamycin complex is unable to bind mTORC2 (Jacinto et al., 2004), although prolonged rapamycin treatment disrupts mTORC2 signaling by preventing mTOR incorporation into mTORC2 (Lamming et al., 2012; Sarbassov et al., 2006).

claim: mTORC2 is activated by growth factors, particularly through the insulin/PI3K signaling pathway

claim: mTORC2 was captured by affinity to a FLAG tag inserted in the amino-terminal HEAT repeats of mTOR

TOR-Lst8 reference yielded classes encompassing free mTOR-mLST8 (30%), mTOR-mLST8 occupied on a single flank by accessory protein (52%) and a complete complex bearing accessory factors on both flanks of the mTOR dimer (18%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
